title: A reckoning on social media addiction came late for many kids. Will AI safety be different?
source_used: Associated Press, text read in the Republican Herald copy (dl14/ap09_rh.txt; AP by Kaitlyn Huamani and Barbara Ortutay, 5 Oct 2026); apnews.com returned 403
key_facts: AP technology writers Kaitlyn Huamani and Barbara Ortutay say that, years after the risks of social media for kids became apparent, US states this summer reached an accord hailed as a turning point for child safety while a new generation of children uses AI.

Meta agreed to changes to its platforms and enhanced safeguards in an $18 billion settlement; parent advocate Kristin Bride said it got at what has been known for years and asked how to get at what is not yet known.
Advocates say the main lesson is to act sooner on AI's harms for kids; University of Chicago physician Dana Suskind hopes society will not 'sleepwalk into this next tech revolution'.

AI companies have been moving somewhat faster than social media firms: OpenAI introduced teen accounts in August, about four years after launching ChatGPT, while Meta did not launch Instagram teen accounts until 2024.

Experts say the Meta settlement's protections cannot easily be applied to AI because teens also use chatbots for tutoring and homework; Cornell's Sarah Kreps said it is much easier to point to AI's upsides than social media's.
64% of US teens say they have used AI chatbots and about 12% have turned to bots for emotional support or advice, according to the Pew Research Center.
Psychologist Jonathan Haidt said he is most worried about attachments to chatbots and 'cognitive offloading', and that AI may be a bigger threat to children than social media.

Some child-safety AI bills (youth privacy, chatbot interactions, AI toy safety) have passed Senate subcommittees with bipartisan support but face a long road; state legislation is moving faster, and the Trump administration says regulation could hinder AI companies' growth.
quote_evidence: AI companies have begun rolling out some safety features introduced first by social media companies, including age assurance measures and restricted experiences for minors.

OpenAI introduced teen accounts in August, about four years after launching ChatGPT, with restrictions that include a ban on romantic chats and any suggestions that the chatbot has personal feelings toward the user.
A majority of U.S. teens — 64% — say they have used AI chatbots, according to the Pew Research Center.
why_it_matters_hint: Advocates argue that AI child-safety rules should not repeat social media's slow start, while the legal and technical fixes differ.
event_date: AP article 5 Oct 2026; the Meta settlement and the US states' accord date from this summer (2026).
